The summer I turned eleven my grandfather let me drive the tractor, which my mother did not find out about until years later. It was an old Ford, more rust than blue, and the seat had a split in it that pinched if you sat wrong. He stood on the hitch behind me with one hand on the fender and told me to keep it straight along the fence line. I did not keep it straight.

We took out maybe six feet of his beans before he reached past me and killed the engine. I remember the quiet after. A meadowlark somewhere. My ears ringing. I was certain he would shout, because my father would have, but he only climbed down, looked at the flattened row for a while, and said, "Well. Those ones were ugly anyway."

He died when I was nineteen. At the funeral a neighbor told me he'd bragged about that day for a decade, how his granddaughter had driven the tractor at eleven and only wrecked a little. I had been ashamed of it the whole time. Funny what people carry for you without saying so.
